diagnosis.what_is_wrong: The coding workload had a short, sustained CPU-heavy execution burst: the newly appearing ttworker cohort consumed nearly four CPU cores continuously, plausibly extending the task's completion time. The trace localizes that work to one container; it does not establish host-wide CPU saturation or a CPU limit/throttling event.
diagnosis.evidence: Compared quiet pre-work activity with the active interval using run_python sched_stat_runtime sums: over 02:49:12.0–14.6 the container averaged about 0.12 CPU cores, versus 15.19 CPU-seconds over 3.8 seconds (3.998 cores) in 02:49:14.7–18.5; ttworker alone accounted for 14.804 CPU-seconds (97.4%). Process-lifetime evidence places the ttworker/xargs/run_all.sh workload cohort at the same boundary. Raw sched_switch and sched_stat_runtime records show ttworker executing on CPUs and roughly 1 ms runtime samples; sampled wakeup/switch records did not show sustained runnable delay. Disk/network activity and sampled block timing do not support I/O as the mechanism, and writeback_pages_written samples were zero. A falsifier would be evidence of sustained wakeup-to-run delay, block latency, or a throttling counter rather than on-CPU execution; the sampled scheduler and block lines were checked, though throttling counters are not available in this trace.
diagnosis.window_evidence: The onset is the first sustained 100-ms CPU buckets at the container's 0.4 CPU-seconds per bucket beginning 02:49:14.700, coincident with ttworker's appearance; the interval ends at 02:49:18.500 when its CPU rate falls sharply and its process cohort ends. Adjacent pre-work CPU averaged roughly 0.12–0.41 cores depending on the exact baseline range, and post-work activity averaged about 0.16 cores.
